title: When Sixty Women Waited, the Hamlins Built a Hospital of Their Own
dek: In 1959 two Sydney gynaecologists met their first fistula patient in Addis Ababa; by 1974 they had built a hospital for that one injury.

story.event: Deciding to build a hospital devoted to obstetric fistula after their hostel overflowed
story.summary: Catherine and Reginald Hamlin arrived in Addis Ababa in 1959 on a three-year contract to set up a midwifery school and found themselves repairing obstetric fistulas. When a hostel they had built in the grounds of the Princess Tsehai hospital overflowed, they obtained land with the emperor's permission, raised the money themselves and opened the Addis Ababa Fistula Hospital, by their own account in 1974, as the revolution began. It and its later regional hospitals went on to treat tens of thousands of women.
paragraphs: In May 1959 Reginald and Catherine Hamlin, gynaecologists from Sydney, landed in Addis Ababa with their six-year-old son. Nobody met them, and they did not start work at once: Reg refused until there was a contract for his wife too, and it was pushed under their door on a Friday night, Catherine later recalled. They had signed for three years, to set up a midwifery school at the Princess Tsehai Memorial Hospital. On their first evening a colleague warned them that the fistula patients would break their hearts.

Neither had ever treated an obstetric fistula, the injury left by days of obstructed labour that leaves a woman incontinent and often shunned. The first, as Catherine remembered her, was a girl of about sixteen in rags, sitting apart in outpatients because of the smell; a simple repair cured her within about two weeks. Word spread. Some thirty women came, then more than a hundred the next year; within three years the couple had operated on 300. When patients could not pay the admission fee, the Hamlins often paid it from their own salaries.

The general hospital could not hold them all. In 1962 the Hamlins built a hostel in its grounds with money given from overseas, and that filled too: at one point sixty women were living there, some for years, waiting for a chance to be operated on. One day, Catherine said, Reg asked her, "Why don't we build our own hospital?" They asked Emperor Haile Selassie for land and raised the money themselves, Reg mostly by writing letters and on speaking tours in America. It took more than a decade.

They opened the Addis Ababa Fistula Hospital in 1974, the year the emperor was deposed in a revolution that brought shooting across the valley and, later, the Red Terror. Mission hospitals were nationalised; the Hamlins kept a low profile and kept operating, and, Catherine said, "we never had an empty bed even through those years." The hospital's own history calls it the only centre in the world then devoted solely to fistula repair. Reg worked there until his death in 1993. Catherine stayed until hers in 2020, by which time the hospital and its regional network were thought to have treated more than 60,000 women.

quote.text: no physician, in so far as he is a physician, considers his own good in what he prescribes, but the good of his patient
quote.source_title: The Republic, tr. Benjamin Jowett, Project Gutenberg eBook #1497
quote.connection: Socrates argues that medicine, as an art, looks only to the patient's good, and that earning a living is a separate matter. The Hamlins paid fees from their own salaries, then built that idea into a whole hospital, from free beds to an open ward where frightened women could watch others come safely out of theatre.

reflection: The Hamlins did not begin with a plan for a hospital. They began with one girl in outpatients, then a hostel, then a hostel too full to work. The decision to build came only when the workaround had plainly stopped working, and even then it took more than ten years of letters while the operating went on.

You probably have something, at work or at home, that still lives in a borrowed corner: a task, a person's need, an idea you keep squeezing in. It is worth noticing whether the corner is still enough, and being patient with yourself about how long a proper room can take to build.
invitation: Pick one thing you keep making room for in a makeshift way and write two sentences on what a proper place for it would look like. Then leave the note alone; you do not have to start building today.

sources.title: Our Founders
sources.supports: Three-year contract with the Ethiopian Government in 1959 to set up a midwifery school; the fellow gynaecologist's warning on the evening of arrival; 300 fistula patients operated on within the first three years; the 1962 hostel in the grounds of the Princess Tsehai built with money donated from overseas; more than a decade's work to establish a fistula hospital; founded in 1974 as the only medical centre in the world then dedicated exclusively to obstetric fistula repair; Reg worked there until his death in 1993.

sources.title: Catherine Hamlin obituary
sources.supports: The 1959 Lancet advertisement and the Princess Tsehai hospital; asking the emperor's personal permission for land and raising all the money themselves; the hospital declared open in 1974, the year the emperor was deposed in a violent revolution; the Nightingale-style ward with the operating room in view so patients could see others come out unharmed; treatment free, paid in the early days from the Hamlins' own salaries; Mamitu Gashe; more than 60,000 women operated on over the decades; Reg's death in 1993.

sources.title: Catherine Hamlin: Grief in Ethiopia as trailblazing Australian doctor dies
sources.supports: Arrival in 1959 with nobody to meet them because the cable arrived three weeks late; the first fistula patient sitting alone in outpatients; Mamitu Gashe treated in 1962 and taken on as staff when the fistula hospital opened in 1974; Reg's death in 1993; the organisation thought to have treated more than 60,000 women; Catherine's death on 18 March 2020 in Addis Ababa.

research_notes: Opening date: Catherine Hamlin herself said 1974 (ABC Talking Heads, 2008, and her Right Livelihood speech), as do the Guardian, the BBC and the hospital's 2015 'Our Founders' page; the Embryo Project (Arizona State University) gives 24 May 1975 as the day the Hamlins opened and named the hospital, and a search snippet of the charity's 2020 obituary gave the same date. The story follows the founder's own account (1974) and records the 1975 date here; the founding decision itself is not in dispute. Arrival: the Guardian says the couple answered the Lancet advertisement in 1959 while Wikipedia says 1958; all sources agree they arrived in 1959, and Catherine gave May 1959. Patient totals disagree by date and scope: Catherine said 30,000 repaired (ABC Sunday Profile, March 2008); the charity's founders page said more than 43,000 (2015); the Embryo Project said more than 30,000 by 2015 at the Addis Ababa hospital; the Guardian and BBC (2020) gave more than 60,000, the BBC hedging with 'it is thought' and both including the regional hospitals opened from 2003. The story uses the 2020 figure with the BBC's hedge and says it covers the hospital and its regional network. Early numbers: Catherine recalled about 30 patients and then over 100 the next year; the founders page gives 300 in the first three years; these are compatible. The Embryo Project says the building was paid for by a £10,000 donation from a New Zealand donor; no second source confirms it, so the story says only that they raised the money themselves (Guardian, Talking Heads). The 'only centre in the world' claim is attributed to the hospital's own history. Reg's question and the 'empty bed' line are Catherine's recollection in the 2008 Talking Heads interview. The Talking Heads and Our Founders pages are cited from the Internet Archive because the original ABC and hamlinfistula.org pages are no longer online. The Plato passage is Socrates' argument to Thrasymachus about the arts; it is applied here by analogy. The company field gives the organisation's name, Hamlin Fistula Ethiopia, because the repeat screen treats a shared company word such as 'hospital' as the same company; the hospital itself is named in the story.
